rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-peak elution window while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. The retention and resolution pattern will guide window trimming and targeted slope or temperature changes.

Only the first pair limits the score, while all peaks already elute within 10 minutes. Raising temperature with the gradient unchanged tests whether temperature-dependent selectivity can resolve that pair without a time penalty.

Slightly flatten the gradient at the best temperature to lift the first pair from R = 1.41 toward full resolution. The last peak has ample margin below 10 minutes, so this could reach the maximum CRF without a time penalty.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a shorter fully resolved method. This gradient slope lies between injections 2 and 3, aiming to retain R ≥ 1.5 for the first pair while bringing the last peak out sooner.

Test a higher starting organic fraction while keeping the slope close to the fully resolved injection 4. This should shorten retention and reveal whether the first pair remains resolved as the gradient window is trimmed.

Restore the lower starting organic fraction and use a slope just steeper than injection 4 to preserve first-pair resolution. Ending the gradient at 0.55 tests whether a short final hold can elute the last compound promptly while reducing the programmed gradient duration.

Test a slightly steeper gradient than injection 6 to locate the shortest fully resolved boundary. The first pair is close to R = 1.5, so this small slope increase will show whether any further time reduction is feasible without losing the maximum score.

Flatten the gradient relative to injection 5 to recover first-pair resolution at the higher starting organic fraction. This tests an alternative trimmed window while retaining the established CRF 1.000 methods as benchmarks.

Test the low-temperature endpoint for an alternative selectivity regime, since unidentified peaks may have exchanged order between 40 and 60 °C. The broad, fast gradient should limit late retention while revealing whether lower temperature can fully resolve the critical pair.

At 25 °C the first pair has excess resolution, but three later peaks cluster tightly. A substantially steeper gradient tests whether differing solvent sensitivities separate that cluster while shortening the run.

The late cluster barely responded to gradient slope at 25 °C, so test a modest temperature increase to change its selectivity. An intermediate gradient duration should preserve more first-pair resolution than the six-minute gradient while keeping elution fast.

Test whether 35 °C separates the late cluster while a shallower gradient restores the early pair’s resolution. This explores an alternative fully resolved temperature regime; injection 6 remains the fastest confirmed method with CRF 1.000.

Test whether a higher starting organic fraction improves early-pair selectivity in the lower-temperature regime. The shorter gradient should reduce retention substantially, while this run checks whether the late cluster remains adequately separated.

Keep injection 13’s starting composition and temperature, but flatten the gradient to improve its sole unresolved pair. The slope matches injection 12 while the higher starting organic fraction should bring the last peak out earlier.

Return to the temperature that consistently achieves maximum CRF and slightly steepen injection 8’s gradient. This should retain first-pair resolution near 1.5 while testing a faster version of that fully resolved method.
